title: Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease Presenting as Expressive Aphasia and Nonconvulsive Status Epilepticus
case_prompt:
A 60-year-old man with benign prostatic hyperplasia presented with a four-week history of progressive speech difficulty—primarily word-finding problems with stuttering—and confusion, including failure to recognize family. Symptoms began with headache, fatigue, and vertigo, then evolved to intermittent confusion, slurred speech, and spasms of the right upper and lower extremities, causing a fall without loss of consciousness. He recently returned from a four-month stay in Mexico working in cattle manure. He had no prior neuropsychiatric history and no family history of dementia or seizures.

Ten days before admission, he had a normal neurologic exam, brain MRI, and carotid Doppler and was diagnosed with transient ischemic attack. On transfer to our emergency department, vital signs were stable; neurologic exam revealed persistent word-finding difficulty only. Noncontrast head CT was unremarkable. Initial CSF showed mildly elevated protein (65 mg/dL) but no clear evidence of infection. He was admitted and treated for complex migraine with ketorolac, sumatriptan, and promethazine. On hospital day 2, EEG demonstrated focal seizures from the left frontal region, and levetiracetam was started. He then developed right upper extremity weakness with diminished reflexes and, on day 3, intermittent myoclonic jerks of the same limb. Metabolic panels, ammonia, liver and renal function, and toxins were normal; medications lowering seizure threshold were discontinued. Despite increasing levetiracetam, he became drowsier with worsening aphasia and cerebellar signs. MRI without contrast on day 3 showed only mild cerebral and cerebellar volume loss. By day 4, EEG still showed left hemispheric seizures; lacosamide was added, and continuous EEG initiated. On day 5, MRI with contrast revealed cytotoxic edema in left frontal and parietal lobes. Given elevated CSF protein and myoclonus, a 3-day course of high-dose steroids was given for possible autoimmune encephalitis. Antiseizure drugs were escalated and valproic acid added. CSF microbiology, oligoclonal bands, and autoimmune panels returned negative; acyclovir was briefly administered and stopped when CSF viral studies were negative. On days 9–11, he remained globally aphasic and flaccid in the right arm; repeat MRI showed persistent cortical ribboning in the left hemisphere, and EEG disclosed diffuse epileptiform discharges with continuous left frontal and bifrontal sharp spikes, concerning for nonconvulsive status epilepticus. Perampanel and phenobarbital were added without improvement.  

At this point, Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease was considered among other etiologies, and CTA, paraneoplastic panels, and repeat CSF studies—including 14-3-3 protein—were planned.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Transient ischemic attack — “he was discharged home with a working diagnosis of transient ischemic attack.”  
2. Complex migraine — “he was admitted to the neurology unit and diagnosed with a complex migraine and treated with intravenous …”  
3. Infectious etiology — “Differential diagnoses, though less likely, included an infectious etiology which was excluded with negative microbiology…”  
4. Stroke — “a stroke despite a normal MRI”  
5. Metabolic causes — “or other common metabolic causes including electrolyte abnormalities, ammonia, toxins, and liver and kidney dysfunction.”  
6. Medication-induced lowered seizure threshold — “Medications were also considered which could potentially lower seizure threshold, and tramadol and diphenhydramine were discontinued.”  
7. Autoimmune encephalitis — “start a 3-day course of pulse dose steroids … for possible autoimmune encephalitis (AE) while awaiting the finalized autoimmune workup”  
8. Viral encephalitis — “Acyclovir was started empirically for possible viral encephalitis but subsequently discontinued two days later when CSF resulted negative.”  
9. Paraneoplastic encephalitis, meningeal carcinomatosis, infectious cerebritis, primary CNS angiitis — “At this point CJD was considered among other possible etiologies such as paraneoplastic encephalitis, meningeal carcinomatous, infectious cerebritis, and primary CNS angiitis.”  
10. Primary CNS angiitis — “Computed tomography angiogram (CTA) excluded the primary central nervous system (CNS) angiitis.”
